explanations.explanation: Yes, and God says it right in the verse. The eagle looms "because the people have transgressed My covenant and rebelled against My law." The reason comes with the warning, so nobody has to guess. When the horn blows, baker, God has already told them why.

explanations.answer: They lost a battle at the border
explanations.explanation: I can see why a war picture comes to mind with an eagle overhead and a horn blowing. But the verse never mentions a lost battle. It gives the reason itself: "the people have transgressed My covenant and rebelled against My law." The trouble is about the covenant, not the border.

The verse says nothing about offerings running short. Later in this very message, God says "Though they offer sacrifices as gifts to Me." So the offerings are still coming in. The reason for the eagle is that the people "rebelled against My law."

I get why this one sounds right, since Israel just said, "O our God, we know You!" But God's answer goes the other direction: "Israel has rejected good; an enemy will pursue him." So Israel did not hold on to what is good. They pushed it away. That's quite a reply to a big claim.

That's right. Israel says, "we know You," and God answers, "Israel has rejected good." Then He adds that "an enemy will pursue him." Saying the words and holding on to the good are two different things, baker.

explanations.answer: They did it without His approval
explanations.explanation: That's it. God says, "They set up kings, but not by Me. They make princes, but without My approval." Israel handled the crowns on its own and left God out of it. Picture someone running your whole bakery schedule and never once asking you.

explanations.answer: They picked kings who were too young
explanations.explanation: The text never says anything about how old these kings were. God's complaint is about who did the choosing: "They set up kings, but not by Me." The princes get the same treatment, "without My approval." Age isn't part of it.

explanations.answer: They taxed the people too hard
explanations.explanation: Taxes never come up in this verse. The complaint is plain: "They set up kings, but not by Me. They make princes, but without My approval." The problem is that God was left out of the choosing. The text doesn't go into how those rulers behaved.

Yes, idols. "With their silver and gold they make themselves idols, to their own destruction." They spent the good stuff on things that couldn't help them. That's like pouring your whole paycheck into a toaster that doesn't toast.

Silver and gold do sound like crown material, I'll give you that. But the verse says "they make themselves idols." The kings and princes come just before it in the same verse, so the mix-up is easy. The silver and gold went into idols, and it was "to their own destruction."

No chariots in this verse, friend. It says, "With their silver and gold they make themselves idols, to their own destruction." Gold and silver spent on idols, and the verse says where that leads. Nothing here rolls on wheels.

True. God says, "For this thing is from Israel—a craftsman made it, and it is not God." So the calf didn't come from heaven. It came from a workshop. Something somebody made can't be the One who made them.
It's the other way around. God says, "For this thing is from Israel—a craftsman made it, and it is not God." So the calf came from Israel's own hands. That's why it can't be God.

I can see why you'd think a big idol would last. But God says the opposite: "It will be broken to pieces, that calf of Samaria." Nothing in the verse says it stands for years. Broken to pieces is the whole forecast.
That's right. God says, "It will be broken to pieces, that calf of Samaria." There's no "standing for years" in that sentence. A thing a craftsman made can be broken, and God says this one will be.

That's the line. "Even if it should produce, the foreigners would swallow it up." First the grain doesn't stand and the sprouts give no flour. And if something does come in, outsiders take it anyway. Talk about no good news at the end of the row.

explanations.answer: It would be stored up for later
explanations.explanation: No storing happens in this verse. God says, "Even if it should produce, the foreigners would swallow it up." Whatever the fields give, someone else eats it. Nothing is left on the shelf for later.

explanations.answer: It would be shared with the poor
explanations.explanation: That would be a happy ending, but it isn't in this verse. The text says, "Even if it should produce, the foreigners would swallow it up." The harvest goes to foreigners. Sharing never comes up.

Assyria, yes. "For they have gone up to Assyria like a wild donkey on its own." A wild donkey doesn't wait for directions, and neither did Israel. They went off on their own, straight to Assyria, a mighty nation.

Babylon is a name you hear a lot in the Bible, so it's an easy one to grab. But this verse names another nation: "For they have gone up to Assyria like a wild donkey on its own." Assyria is where Israel heads, baker.

Moab doesn't show up in this verse. It says, "For they have gone up to Assyria like a wild donkey on its own." Assyria is the answer. Israel isn't just wandering, because the text points to a specific place.

True. God says, "Though they hire allies among the nations, I will now round them up." They paid for friends among the nations, and God still says He will round them up. The hired help can't change that.

This one is true, friend. The verse says, "Though they hire allies among the nations, I will now round them up." The "though" matters here. Even with allies they paid for, God says He will round them up.

Strange is the word. "Though I wrote for them the great things of My law, they regarded them as something strange." God wrote them out, and Israel treated them like they came from another planet. Even a cookie planet knows better than that.

Sacred is how they should have treated it, but that's not what the verse says. God says, "they regarded them as something strange." He wrote out the great things of His law for them, and they saw it as odd. That's the sting of it.

Beautiful would be a lovely response. But the verse says, "they regarded them as something strange." God wrote the great things of His law for them, and they didn't take it that way. Strange is the word the text uses.

I see why you might say that, since they are offering sacrifices and even eating the meat. But God says, "the LORD does not accept them." The gifts are real, and the answer is still no. The next part says He will "remember their iniquity and punish their sins."

Right. God says, "Though they offer sacrifices as gifts to Me, and though they eat the meat, the LORD does not accept them." They bring the gifts and eat the meat, but the LORD does not accept them. After that He says He will remember their iniquity and punish their sins.

Egypt. God says, "They will return to Egypt." The word "return" is the sad part, since Egypt is a place Israel's story had already left. The verse says it right after He promises to "remember their iniquity and punish their sins."

Edom is a neighbor in the Bible, but it isn't named here. The verse says, "They will return to Egypt." It follows God's words about remembering their iniquity and punishing their sins. Egypt is the answer.
Ur isn't mentioned anywhere in this passage. God says, "They will return to Egypt." That comes right after He says He will "remember their iniquity and punish their sins." Egypt is the place.

Fire. God says, "I will send fire upon their cities, and it will consume their citadels." Israel built palaces and Judah multiplied its fortified cities. Walls and palaces look strong, but the verse says fire will consume the citadels.

A flood is a big, dramatic guess, but it isn't what the verse says. God says, "I will send fire upon their cities, and it will consume their citadels." The palaces and fortified cities get fire, not water.

Locusts show up in other parts of the Bible, but not in this verse. God says, "I will send fire upon their cities, and it will consume their citadels." Fire is the answer here. It lands on the cities Israel and Judah built up.
